incumbent.name: Dave Hall
incumbent.summary: Dave Hall, a Norman Republican who farms and owns a crop insurance agency, has represented House District 62 since 2022 {caucus_hall}. He is an assistant majority whip and vice chair of the House Utilities, Energy and Telecommunications Committee {caucus_hall}.
record: Committees: Utilities, Energy and Telecommunications (vice chair); Local Government; Natural Resources; appointed to the Interim Study Committee on Energy, Utilities and Telecommunications in 2025 and 2026 {caucus_hall}.

2023 session: Sponsored HB 1281, which would require high school students to show proficiency in personal financial literacy to graduate, starting with the Class of 2027; the House passed it in February 2023 {caucus_hb1281}.

2024 session: Authored HEA 1108, signed in March 2024, which bars local governments from prohibiting development on slopes under 25%; Monroe County had limited building on slopes over 15% since 2015 {ipm_slopes}. Hall said the goal was to "free up more land for development"; Monroe County's planning director raised concerns about erosion and enforcement costs, and Sen. Sue Glick (R-LaGrange) voted no, calling it state overreach {ipm_slopes}. Co-sponsored SEA 5 (2024) on lead water service line replacement {caucus_sea5}.

2025 session: Authored HB 1458 ("Sunny's Bill") to let healthy dogs and cats retired from research labs be adopted; it passed the House in February 2025 {caucus_hb1458}. Co-authored HEA 1007, which creates incentives for small modular nuclear reactors {caucus_laws_2025}.

April 10, 2025: Voted yes when the House passed SEA 1, the 2025 property-tax law, 65-29 {rc_sea1_433}. April 25, 2025: Voted yes on the 2025 state budget conference report (HEA 1001), adopted 66-27 {rc_hb1001_576}.

Dec. 5, 2025: Voted no on HB 1032, the mid-decade congressional redistricting bill, which passed the House 57-41; he was one of the Republicans voting no {rc_hb1032_28}. No public explanation of the vote by Hall was found.

2026 session: Voted yes on final House passage of HEA 1002 on utility rates, 94-2 {rc_hb1002_293}, and wrote in September 2026 that it adds performance incentives for utilities, low-income assistance programs and summer disconnection protections {caucus_energy_col}. Authored HB 1204, a $1 state park entry charge to fund public safety in counties hosting state parks and lakes; it cleared the Natural Resources Committee but did not become law {caucus_hb1204} {caucus_hall_2026}.

race_context: House District 62 includes all of Brown County and parts of Monroe and Jackson counties {caucus_hall}. The Oliver campaign describes the Monroe portion as parts of six townships outside Bloomington and the Jackson portion as Owen, Pershing and Salt Creek townships {oliver_faq}.

The seat has been close: Hall's 2022 opponent lost by 40 votes {ipm_slopes}, and in 2024 Hall beat Democrat Thomas Horrocks by just under 800 votes, per unofficial results {ipm_2024}, with 51.1% {wiki_2026}. Wikipedia reports Kamala Harris carried the district by 0.3% in 2024 {wiki_2026}.

Hall and Oliver were each the only candidate listed in their party's May 5, 2026 primary {wiki_2026}; both are on the November ballot {in_list}. The Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee lists the race as a target {dlcc_oliver}.

Data centers have become a point of dispute: in a campaign letter, Hall says his opponent has questioned his record and his financial disclosure on the topic; he says siting decisions should be made locally and that he has no interest in any Indiana data center project {hall_letter}. Oliver's campaign says data centers should "pay their own way and get community support" {oliver_site}.

Key differences: Oliver calls for cutting the state sales tax on home utility bills and reversing school funding cuts {oliver_site} {oliver_priorities}; Hall voted for the 2025 budget and property-tax law {rc_hb1001_576} {rc_sea1_433} and emphasizes addiction treatment, rural internet and opposing involuntary annexation {hall_issues}.
No debate or forum for this race was found.

candidates.summary: Amy Huffman Oliver is a Brown County family law attorney and second-term Brown County school board member who previously worked as a domestic violence prosecutor and a public school teacher {oliver_about}. Her campaign focuses on utility costs, school funding and health care {oliver_priorities}.
background: Family law attorney and mediator; previously a domestic violence prosecutor in Marion and Monroe counties, legal director of Turning Point Domestic Violence Services in Columbus, a deputy attorney general in the Consumer Protection Division and an administrative law judge for unemployment appeals {oliver_about}.
After 20 years as an attorney, taught U.S. history and government at CSA New Tech High School in Columbus and seventh-grade world history at Brown County Junior High {oliver_about}.

Elected to the Brown County Schools board in 2020 and 2024; serves on the Indiana School Boards Association legislative committee {oliver_about}. Graduated from Columbus North High School, Smith College and the Indiana University School of Law in Bloomington; lives in Brown County {oliver_about}.
path_to_ballot: Was unopposed in the May 5, 2026 Democratic primary {wiki_2026} {oliver_primary}. Her campaign says she drew more primary votes than Hall, and more than three times as many in Monroe County {oliver_primary}.

items: Supports ending the state sales tax on home utility bills, which her campaign says would save the average family about "$350 a year" {oliver_priorities}.

Says utilities wanting new technology should pay for it until it produces energy, rather than customers, and that the state should ensure "big companies do not make too much profit" {oliver_priorities}.

Says data centers should "pay their own way and get community support" {oliver_site}; her fundraising page lists opposing data centers proposed for local communities among her priorities {oliver_actblue}.
Supports fully funding public schools by "reversing damaging funding cuts" and raising teacher and staff pay {oliver_site} {oliver_priorities}.
Says all schools receiving tax money should follow the same rules and that local school boards, not the legislature, should make local decisions {oliver_priorities}.

Says "Recent cuts to Medicaid have made things harder for families, people with disabilities, and seniors" and that some small-town hospitals risk closing; supports preventive care and more in-home health services {oliver_priorities}.
Her fundraising page lists access to "a full range of reproductive healthcare" among her priorities {oliver_actblue}.

on_incumbent: Her campaign's fundraising page says Democrats lost the district "by a tiny margin" in 2022 and 2024 and that she will not accept donations from utility and construction PACs, "unlike her opponent" {oliver_actblue}.

Hall's campaign letter says his opponent has repeatedly criticized his data center record and cited stocks in his financial disclosure; Oliver's own statements on this were not found on her website {hall_letter}.
plans: Says she will focus on lowering the cost of gas, housing, utilities and everyday essentials {oliver_site}.
Says her goal is to "make things better and more affordable for Hoosiers" {oliver_primary}.
endorsements_finance: Endorsed by the Indiana AFL-CIO, AFT Indiana, Planned Parenthood Alliance Advocates, the Indiana Reproductive Freedom PAC and Stonewall Democrats of South Central Indiana; listed as recommended by IPACE (Indiana Political Action Committee for Education) {oliver_endorse}.
Listed as a Target Race by the Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee {dlcc_oliver} {oliver_endorse}.
gaps: Campaign finance totals were not found.
Her specific statements about Hall's data center record and financial disclosure (as described in Hall's letter) were not found; likely on social media or in mailers.
Indiana Capital Chronicle voter guide (403) could not be read; search snippets indicate she said she does not support eliminating property and/or gas taxes — unverified.
No position found on the 2025 property-tax law (SEA 1) or congressional redistricting.

candidates.summary: Dave Hall is the Republican incumbent, first elected in 2022 {caucus_hall}. His recent work has centered on utility rates and energy, rural public safety funding and housing supply {caucus_energy_col} {caucus_hb1204} {ipm_slopes}.
background: Farms about 500 acres of corn and soybeans with his father and owns Dave Hall Crop Insurance; graduated from Brownstown Central High School {caucus_hall}.

Former president of the Jackson County Council; serves on the Jackson County REMC board and as a special deputy with the Jackson County Sheriff's Department {caucus_hall}. Lives in northwest Jackson County {hall_site}.
path_to_ballot: Was the only candidate listed in the May 5, 2026 Republican primary {wiki_2026}.

items: Wrote that "Every Hoosier needs electricity, so keeping it reliable and affordable must remain a priority," and that HEA 1002 ties utility incentives to affordability and service restoration {caucus_energy_col}.
Said HEA 1007's nuclear incentives are "a smart step forward as we work to meet growing energy needs" {caucus_laws_2025}.
Says data center decisions "should be made locally" and that a state study is examining effects on farmland, water, energy and taxpayers {hall_letter}.
Says he did not vote for Indiana's 2019 data center tax incentive and that the bill he supported added quantum research and defense technology to state law, citing NSWC Crane {hall_letter}.

Said HEA 1108 (2024) aimed to "free up more land for development" to expand housing supply {ipm_slopes}; called housing "A top concern for Brown County residents" in describing the 2026 housing law (HEA 1001) {caucus_bc_col}.
Called his state park fee bill "a commonsense step to address the unique needs of counties" that host parks and lakes {caucus_hb1204}.
Lists combating drug abuse and mental health problems as a priority, citing the Jackson-Jennings Work Release Center he helped start {hall_issues}.
Says "Annexation should be voluntary" and that the burden should rest on the municipality {hall_issues}.
Lists improving infrastructure and rural high-speed internet as a priority {hall_issues}.

on_incumbent: In a campaign letter, Hall says his opponent has mischaracterized his record on data centers several times and has cited stocks in his candidate financial disclosure; he says the holdings are among about 150 publicly traded companies in his retirement fund and that he has no ownership or private interest in any Indiana data center project {hall_letter}.
plans: Says he will keep examining ways to improve the consistency and accountability of Indiana's utilities before the next session {caucus_energy_col}.
Campaign priorities: drug abuse and mental health, infrastructure and internet reliability, and limiting government overreach {hall_issues}.
endorsements_finance: No endorsements are listed on his campaign website {hall_site}.
gaps: Campaign finance totals were not found.
Whether HB 1281 (2023, financial literacy) and HB 1458 (2025, research animal adoption) became law was not confirmed.
No public explanation found for his no vote on HB 1032 (redistricting).
The specific 'bill I did support' on data centers/quantum research referenced in his letter was not identified by number.
Indiana Capital Chronicle voter guide (403) could not be read; snippets say he did not answer its question on eliminating property and gas taxes — unverified.
